Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Event Recall: Talking about the event, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Alcohol Use: drink alcohol, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Vignette:
Helena is a 74-year-old European American woman who has been married for decades and spent most of her adult life working as a physical therapist. When she speaks about why she is finally seeking help now, she does so cautiously, circling the story before entering it, because talking directly about what happened has always been one of the quickest ways to feel as if she is no longer in the present. She came to the United States as a refugee when she was young, after a fire during a period of violent upheaval forced her family to flee their home. What remains most sharply with her is not a tidy narrative but a cluster of sensory moments: the burned smell in the air, the sting of alcohol from spilled spirits and disinfectant in a crowded shelter, the sound of people shouting and pounding and the feeling that someone might come through a door at any second. In her memory, the event is still made of pictures more than words: flames reflected on a wall, a doorway, bodies pressed together, her mother’s face turned toward the sound outside. When the memory comes, she does not experience it as something she is remembering from long ago. For a few moments it is as if it is happening again.

In the years after resettlement, Helena built a life that outwardly looked steady and successful. She married, raised a family, and became known as a reliable, attentive physical therapist. Yet even during those stable years, certain experiences could abruptly pull her back. If someone opened a bottle of liquor nearby and the smell of alcohol drifted toward her, she would stiffen before she could explain why. The odor did not register to her as neutral; it belonged to fear. The smell of something burnt was worse. A scorched pan in a staff break room, a neighbor using a grill, even a faint electrical smell in the clinic could bring on a rush of vivid images so immediate that she would stop what she was doing and look around as though she had been transported into danger. At times she also heard, in her mind, the same sounds from that time long ago—shouting, banging, people trying to get in—and her whole body responded before she could remind herself where she was.

Helena has come to believe that it is safest to stay alert. At home, especially at night, she listens for sounds that might mean someone is entering the house. A settling floorboard, wind against a window, the rattle of a doorknob in another room can make her heart kick up as though an intruder is already inside. She gets up to check locks, checks the windows, then checks them again. During the day she scans her surroundings almost continuously, noticing who is near her, where exits are, whether anyone is approaching too quickly. Strangers feel especially dangerous to her, even in ordinary situations. If a man she does not know steps too close in a grocery aisle or someone approaches her unexpectedly in a parking lot after work, she reacts as if she must protect herself immediately. She knows, afterward, that many of these moments are false alarms, but in the moment they do not feel false at all.

Her work as a physical therapist has given these reactions many opportunities to surface. In the clinic, patients’ family members and delivery workers move in and out all day, and Helena finds herself tracking them before she can focus fully on the person in front of her. If a patient arrives having used hand sanitizer with a sharp alcohol scent, or if burnt coffee drifts from the staff lounge, she may lose the thread of a session and feel flooded by images. She has managed for years by keeping her face composed, but the effort has grown more exhausting with age. At home, she sometimes pours herself alcohol in the evening, describing it less as enjoyment than as a way to take the edge off after a day spent bracing. Just as often, she sits dwelling on who she used to be before the event—someone she imagines as more carefree, less watchful, less ruled by sudden jolts of fear.

Over the months before seeking treatment, these patterns became harder to contain. Her husband noticed that she was making more rounds through the house at night and startling more intensely at small noises. At work, after catching a burnt smell from a malfunctioning toaster in the break room, she had to step into an empty office because the images came so fast and vividly that she felt disoriented. What finally brought her in was not one new symptom but her growing sense that the past still has too much access to her present life. She is frightened by how quickly ordinary smells, conversations about her history, or an unfamiliar person coming toward her can make the world feel unsafe. At the same time, she is hoping—carefully, skeptically—that speaking here might help her tell the story without being pulled all the way back into it, and that she might someday sit in her own home or move through her clinic without listening so hard for danger.
